blocks.text: Proteins are linear chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. A peptide bond is an amide bond formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, with loss of water. The long chains formed by many peptide links are polypeptide chains, and each protein has specific polypeptide chains that determine its structure and function. Proteins are organised at four structural levels.

Primary structure: the specific sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. This sequence decides how the protein folds into its three-dimensional shape, and so its function; even one changed amino acid can impair the protein. Proteins such as albumin and insulin depend on precise sequences. In sickle-cell anaemia an abnormal haemoglobin makes red blood cells sickle-shaped; the sickle cells clog blood vessels and disturb circulation.

blocks.alt: Two amino acids, H2N-CH(R)-COOH and H2N-CH(R')-COOH; the OH of the first acid's COOH and an H of the second acid's NH2 are ringed. An arrow leads to the dipeptide, in which the C=O and N-H joined between them are boxed as the 'Peptide linkage', + H2O. Below, a long chain of coloured beads stands for a polypeptide chain.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.4: The peptide chain formation by the peptide bonds between amino acids (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.4).

blocks.text: Secondary structure: the backbone atoms form hydrogen bonds (between C=O and N-H groups) within or between chains, giving regular patterns. In an alpha-helix the hydrogen bonds form along a single chain, giving a coiled spiral (e.g. keratin); in a beta-pleated sheet they form between neighbouring strands, giving a folded sheet (e.g. silk fibroin).

blocks.alt: Top: a beta pleated sheet of three chains lying on pleated folds; carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen atoms and R group side chains are shown, with dashed hydrogen bonds between the C=O of one chain and the N-H of the next. A legend names carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, R group side chain, hydrogen and hydrogen bond. Bottom: an alpha-helix ribbon with C=O...H-N between turns, beside the note on the hydrogen bonds per turn.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.5: Formation of alpha-helix and beta pleated sheets from the primary amino acid chains (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.5).
blocks.long_description: The note beside the helix reads: The turns of the helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups in the peptide links. Each turn has 3-4 hydrogen bonds holding it to the next turn.

blocks.text: Tertiary structure: the overall three-dimensional shape formed when a chain folds because of interactions between side chains (R groups): hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulphide bridges. This shape decides the function; in enzymes, the exact shape of the active site allows the substrate to bind.

blocks.alt: Left: a bead chain with an arrow at its start, labelled Primary structure, the order in which the amino acids are linked in the chain. Yellow arrows lead to an alpha-helix and a beta-pleated sheet, labelled Secondary structure, the coiling or folding of the primary structure. Further arrows lead to a folded chain of helices, sheets and loops, labelled Tertiary structure.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.6: From primary amino acid chains to tertiary structure of proteins (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.6).

blocks.text: Quaternary structure: in some proteins two or more folded chains (subunits) associate through hydrogen bonds, ionic (salt) bridges, hydrophobic interactions and sometimes disulphide bonds.
By overall shape, proteins are divided into two classes:

items: Fibrous proteins: long, rod-like or thread-like molecules whose chains run parallel and are linked by strong hydrogen bonds or disulphide bonds into fibres. They are generally insoluble in water, mechanically strong and stable, and act as structural polymers, e.g. collagen (connective tissue), keratin (hair, nails, skin) and myosin (muscle). Keratin of hair and the fibroin of silk are fibrous proteins.

Globular proteins: the whole molecule is spherical or oval. Most 'worker' (functional) proteins, such as enzymes, hormones and nutrient proteins, are globular. They are more sensitive to heat and pH: egg white hardens on heating because the hydrogen bonds between chains are broken and the chains open up, and the milk protein casein coagulates when lemon juice lowers the pH. This is denaturation of proteins.
